subject: English

topics.name: Listening and responding
topics.description: Listening involves attending to a speaker and responding to what they have communicated, including through spoken, signed or supported communication.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Oral Language; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: listening and responding.
evidence: Responds to another person's message with a relevant comment or question.
misconceptions: Listening only means being quiet.
topics.question: A friend says, “I like the blue kite because it flies high.” What could you ask them?
topics.answer: For example, “Where do you fly your kite?”
topics.explanation: The question picks up the friend's idea and invites them to add information.
hints: What did the friend mention?
Ask for one detail about the kite.
topics.activity: Take turns describing a favourite object; the listener asks a related question before swapping roles.

topics.name: Asking Questions
topics.description: Questions help a learner obtain information or clarify something they did not understand.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Oral Language; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: asking questions.
evidence: Asks a relevant question and identifies the information sought.
misconceptions: A question and a statement do exactly the same job.
topics.question: Someone says they saw a bird at the beach. Ask a question that would help you find out more.
topics.answer: For example, “What did the bird look like?”
topics.explanation: A useful question asks for information missing from the original statement.
hints: What detail is missing?
Try beginning with what, where, when or how.
topics.activity: Look at an outdoor picture together and take turns asking questions about things you cannot yet tell.

topics.name: Single Letter Sounds
topics.description: Letters represent speech sounds, and the same written letter can represent different sounds in different words. Start with a taught sound–letter correspondence.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: single letter sounds.
evidence: Identifies a taught letter–sound correspondence in a familiar word.
misconceptions: The name of a letter is always the sound it represents in a word.
topics.question: What sound does the letter m represent at the start of “mat”?
topics.explanation: In this word the first letter represents the initial /m/ sound.
hints: Say “mat” slowly.
Hold the first sound before saying the rest.
topics.activity: Place three picture cards on a table and find the ones beginning with a sound the child has been taught.

topics.name: Blending Sounds to Read Words
topics.description: A reader can blend individual sounds in order to recognise a word. Work with sound–letter correspondences already taught.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: blending sounds to read words.
evidence: Blends the individual sounds of a simple taught word.
misconceptions: A word must be guessed from the picture without checking its letters.
topics.question: Blend /s/ /a/ /t/. What word do you hear?
topics.answer: sat.
topics.explanation: The three sounds are joined in order to form the spoken word.
hints: Say the sounds in order.
Say them again with shorter gaps between sounds.
topics.activity: Use three counters for the sounds in a few familiar words, sliding the counters together while blending.

topics.name: Rhyming words
topics.description: Rhyming words share the same final sound pattern even if they begin differently.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: rhyming words.
evidence: Recognises and produces a spoken rhyme.
misconceptions: Words rhyme because they begin with the same sound.
topics.question: Do “cat” and “hat” rhyme? What part sounds alike?
topics.answer: Yes. Both end with the sound /at/.
topics.explanation: Their final spoken sounds match.
hints: Listen to how each word ends.
Compare cat with hat, then cat with dog.
topics.activity: Say three familiar words and sort the two that rhyme; invite the learner to suggest another.

topics.name: Characters, settings, and events
topics.description: Stories introduce people or other characters, a setting and events. Readers can use words and illustrations as evidence.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: characters, settings, and events.
evidence: Identifies a character, a setting and an event from a text.
misconceptions: A setting is always the name of a character.
topics.question: In “Ari found a shell on the beach,” who is the character and where is the setting?
topics.answer: Ari is the character; the beach is the setting.
topics.explanation: The sentence names who did something and where it happened.
hints: Who found the shell?
Which words tell you where?
topics.activity: Read a short story and draw one character, the setting and an event; point to evidence in the story.

topics.name: Retelling Stories with Structure
topics.description: Retelling puts important events in an order that helps another person understand the story.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: retelling stories with structure.
evidence: Retells key events in a clear sequence.
misconceptions: A retelling needs every tiny detail and can change the order.
topics.question: A seed is planted, watered and then sprouts. What happened first and what happened last?
topics.answer: First the seed was planted; last it sprouted.
topics.explanation: A retelling keeps the order of the events.
hints: Which action made the seed ready to grow?
Which event came after watering?
topics.activity: After sharing a short story, draw three moments and explain them in order.

topics.name: Saying Sentences Before Writing Them
topics.description: Saying or signing a complete idea before writing helps a beginner hold the sentence in mind while composing and recording it.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: saying sentences before writing them.
evidence: Communicates a complete sentence before attempting to record it.
misconceptions: Writing can only begin once every spelling is already known.
topics.question: Say a sentence about a dog sleeping. What complete idea would you write?
topics.answer: For example, “The dog is asleep.”
topics.explanation: The sentence names something and says what is happening.
hints: Who or what is your sentence about?
What is the dog doing?
topics.activity: Say or communicate one sentence, count its words with fingers or counters, then write it with support.

topics.name: Spelling from Dictation
topics.description: A writer can listen to a short word, identify its sounds in order and select taught letters or letter groups to spell it.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: spelling from dictation.
evidence: Segments a familiar word and selects appropriate taught letters.
misconceptions: Writing the first sound alone records the whole word.
topics.question: What sounds do you hear in “sun”, and what letters could represent them?
topics.answer: /s/ /u/ /n/, written s-u-n.
topics.explanation: The letters record the sounds in the order heard.
hints: Say the word slowly.
Listen for the first, middle and last sounds.
topics.activity: Use counters to represent sounds in familiar words, then replace them with taught letters.

topics.name: Simple Stories with Beginning and Ending
topics.description: A simple story can introduce a situation, describe what happens and bring the event to an end.
topics.locator: Phase 1 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: simple stories with beginning and ending.
evidence: Creates an ending that connects to earlier events.
misconceptions: An ending can ignore what happened earlier in the story.
topics.question: A boy loses his hat and finds it under a chair. How could the story end?
topics.answer: For example, “He put his hat back on and went outside.”
topics.explanation: The ending resolves the small problem introduced earlier.
hints: What problem does the story start with?
How might the character feel after finding the hat?
topics.activity: Fold a page into three spaces and draw or write a beginning, a problem and an ending.

topics.name: Group discussions
topics.description: Group discussion involves sharing ideas, making room for others and building on what has been said.
topics.locator: Phase 2 teaching sequence > Oral Language; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: group discussions.
evidence: Contributes a relevant idea and responds respectfully to another participant.
misconceptions: A discussion is successful only when one person talks the most.
topics.question: Your group is choosing a class activity. How could you respond when someone suggests a game?
topics.answer: For example, “That sounds fun. Could we choose a game everyone can join?”
topics.explanation: The response acknowledges the idea and adds a relevant consideration.
hints: Begin by recognising the idea.
Add a question or reason that moves the discussion on.
topics.activity: Discuss two possible activities and practise inviting a quiet participant to contribute without putting them on the spot.

topics.name: Expressing & Justifying Opinions
topics.description: An opinion becomes more useful to an audience when it is supported by a relevant reason or example.
topics.locator: Phase 2 teaching sequence > Oral Language; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: expressing & justifying opinions.
evidence: States a position and supports it with a relevant reason.
misconceptions: Any statement following “because” is automatically a relevant reason.
topics.question: Would a library or a playground improve a neighbourhood? Give a choice and one reason.
topics.answer: Either choice can work if a reason supports it; for example, a library offers books and a quiet place to learn.
topics.explanation: The reason must relate to the proposed choice.
hints: Choose one option.
Explain one benefit of that option.
topics.activity: Each person selects an option and gives a reason, then asks a follow-up question about the other view.

topics.name: Inferring Characters' Feelings and Motives
topics.description: A reader combines clues in a text with relevant knowledge to infer a character's likely feelings or motives.
topics.locator: Phase 2 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: inferring characters' feelings and motives.
evidence: Gives a plausible inference and identifies a text clue.
misconceptions: An inference is merely an unsupported guess.
topics.question: “Mia hid the invitation in her bag and smiled.” What might Mia feel, and what is one clue?
topics.answer: She might feel pleased or excited; the smile is a clue. Other reasonable interpretations can be discussed.
topics.explanation: An inference is a supported possibility, not a detail the text directly states.
hints: What did Mia do?
Which action could suggest a feeling?
topics.activity: Use a short passage and highlight a clue, then explain two possible interpretations and what would distinguish them.

topics.name: Main Ideas & Note-Taking
topics.description: Notes capture key ideas in a reader's own words so information can be retrieved and used later.
topics.locator: Phase 2 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: main ideas & note-taking.
evidence: Identifies a main idea and records relevant supporting points.
misconceptions: A main idea is always the first sentence regardless of content.
topics.question: A paragraph explains that wetlands store water, provide habitat and filter sediment. What is its main idea?
topics.answer: Wetlands perform several useful environmental roles.
topics.explanation: The main idea covers the related details without repeating every example.
hints: What subject connects all three details?
Write one short sentence that includes the group of ideas.
topics.activity: Read a short factual paragraph, choose three key words, and use them to explain the main idea aloud.

topics.name: Combining information from texts
topics.description: Readers can combine information from two sources to build a fuller picture and note where the sources differ.
topics.locator: Phase 2 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: combining information from texts.
evidence: Combines relevant information from two texts accurately.
misconceptions: Combining sources means assuming every source says the same thing.
topics.question: One text says a bird eats insects; another says it nests in tree hollows. What can you learn from both?
topics.answer: The bird eats insects and may nest in tree hollows.
topics.explanation: The combined statement keeps each source's contribution and does not invent a connection.
hints: What does the first source tell you?
What new detail does the second add?
topics.activity: Compare two short descriptions of the same topic and use two columns to record what each contributes.

topics.name: Organising Writing into Paragraphs
topics.description: A paragraph groups related sentences around an idea; a new paragraph can signal a change of focus.
topics.locator: Phase 2 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: organising writing into paragraphs.
evidence: Groups related sentences into paragraphs with distinct focuses.
misconceptions: Paragraph breaks are used only when a page is full.
topics.question: Where would a writer start a new paragraph when moving from describing a place to explaining how to care for it?
topics.answer: At the change from description to care actions.
topics.explanation: The two groups of sentences have different organising ideas.
hints: What does the first group describe?
Where does the focus change?
topics.activity: Write two short paragraphs about a familiar place, one describing it and one suggesting how to look after it.

topics.name: Revising and editing
topics.description: Revising improves meaning and organisation; editing checks conventions such as spelling and punctuation.
topics.locator: Phase 2 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: revising and editing.
evidence: Makes a content improvement and a separate convention correction.
misconceptions: Editing and revising only mean copying a draft neatly.
topics.question: A draft says “the dog run home” and skips why the dog left. What is one revision and one edit?
topics.answer: Add an explanation of why the dog left; change “run” to “ran” and add a capital and full stop.
topics.explanation: The added idea clarifies the event; the language changes correct the sentence.
hints: What information is missing?
Which word form or punctuation needs checking?
topics.activity: Read a short draft aloud, add one useful detail, and then check sentence boundaries and spelling.

topics.name: Basic Informational Writing
topics.description: Informational writing introduces a topic and organises relevant facts so a reader can understand it.
topics.locator: Phase 2 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: basic informational writing.
evidence: Organises relevant facts under meaningful headings.
misconceptions: A list of unrelated facts is already a clearly organised explanation.
topics.question: What two headings might help a reader learn about a local bird?
topics.answer: For example, “What it eats” and “Where it lives”.
topics.explanation: The headings group different kinds of information about the same topic.
hints: What might a reader want to know?
Choose two distinct categories.
topics.activity: Choose a familiar plant or bird, verify two facts from a reliable source and write them under helpful headings.

topics.name: Preparing for and Explaining in Discussions
topics.description: A discussion participant can prepare relevant information, explain an idea and ask follow-up questions that test understanding.
topics.locator: Phase 3 teaching sequence > Oral Language; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: preparing for and explaining in discussions.
evidence: Uses a relevant follow-up question to clarify or test a claim.
misconceptions: Asking a question automatically means disagreeing with the speaker.
topics.question: Someone claims a new bus stop will help the community. What question could test that idea?
topics.answer: For example, “Who would be able to use it, and how often would the bus run?”
topics.explanation: The question asks for relevant details needed to judge the claim.
hints: What information would show who benefits?
Ask about access or frequency.
topics.activity: Choose a local proposal and prepare one reason, one possible concern and one respectful follow-up question.

topics.name: Drawing Conclusions from Discussion
topics.description: A conclusion from a discussion brings together relevant points and recognises evidence as well as uncertainty.
topics.locator: Phase 3 teaching sequence > Oral Language; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: drawing conclusions from discussion.
evidence: Summarises discussion points and identifies a limitation in the evidence.
misconceptions: One person's opinion proves the outcome for everyone.
topics.question: Two classmates report that their walk to school is safer with a crossing, but no traffic counts were collected. What is a careful conclusion?
topics.answer: They consider the crossing helpful, but more evidence would be needed to judge the overall safety effect.
topics.explanation: The conclusion separates the participants' views from a wider claim that needs further evidence.
hints: What did the students actually report?
What information is still missing?
topics.activity: After a short discussion, write a conclusion and mark which part is supported and which part remains uncertain.

topics.name: Synthesising across multiple texts
topics.description: Synthesis connects information from different texts to form a supported understanding that goes beyond listing separate details.
topics.locator: Phase 3 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: synthesising across multiple texts.
evidence: Connects evidence from sources while distinguishing possibility from proof.
misconceptions: Two related facts always prove a cause-and-effect relationship.
topics.question: One source reports more people cycling after a path opened; another describes safer crossings on the same route. What tentative connection could you investigate?
topics.answer: The path and crossings might have helped make cycling more accessible, but the sources do not prove cause.
topics.explanation: The sources offer a possible connection; other changes could also explain the increase.
hints: What does each source contribute?
Does the evidence prove why the change occurred?
topics.activity: Compare two short sources on a shared topic, write one combined insight and list an unanswered question.

topics.name: Using Multiple Sources
topics.description: Using more than one source can reveal agreement, differences and gaps. A reader should consider who produced each source and why.
topics.locator: Phase 3 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: using multiple sources.
evidence: Checks authorship, purpose and evidence across sources.
misconceptions: A source is reliable simply because it appears online.
topics.question: A council page and an advertisement make different claims about a park. What should you check?
topics.answer: Check who produced each source, what evidence they provide and whether the information is current.
topics.explanation: The source's purpose and supporting evidence help a reader weigh its claims.
hints: Who is speaking in each source?
What evidence supports each claim?
topics.activity: Compare two short accounts of the same place, noting author, purpose and a question to verify.

topics.name: Figurative Language and Literary Devices
topics.description: A writer may use comparison or imagery to create an effect beyond the literal meanings of individual words.
topics.locator: Phase 3 teaching sequence > Reading; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: figurative language and literary devices.
evidence: Explains a figurative phrase and its effect in context.
misconceptions: Figurative language must always be interpreted literally.
topics.question: What does “the wind whispered through the trees” suggest?
topics.answer: It suggests a soft, quiet sound; the wind is described as if it could whisper.
topics.explanation: The image gives a sound a human action to help the reader imagine its quality.
hints: Can wind literally whisper like a person?
What sort of sound does “whispered” suggest?
topics.activity: Find a figurative phrase in a short text and explain what it suggests and how it changes the mood.

topics.name: Choosing Form and Tone for Your Audience
topics.description: Writers choose form, detail and tone based on their audience and purpose.
topics.locator: Phase 3 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: choosing form and tone for your audience.
evidence: Adjusts language and content for a stated audience and purpose.
misconceptions: One tone and level of detail suits every audience.
topics.question: How might an invitation to a friend differ from a notice for the whole school?
topics.answer: The invitation might use a familiar tone; the notice should clearly give details the wider audience needs.
topics.explanation: The audience affects language choices and how much context to provide.
hints: Who will read each message?
What information might the wider audience need?
topics.activity: Write an invitation and a school notice for the same event, then compare tone, detail and layout.

topics.name: Cohesion and Transitions Across Writing
topics.description: Cohesive writing helps readers follow relationships between ideas using clear references and appropriate transitions.
topics.locator: Phase 3 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: cohesion and transitions across writing.
evidence: Selects a transition that matches the relationship between ideas.
misconceptions: Adding any linking word improves a text even when the relationship is wrong.
topics.question: Which transition fits: “The route is longer. ___, it avoids a steep hill.”?
topics.answer: “However” can show a contrast between length and avoiding the hill.
topics.explanation: The transition signals how the second point relates to the first.
hints: Do the two ideas add to each other or contrast?
Choose a word that signals contrast.
topics.activity: Reorder three short paragraphs and add transitions that accurately express their relationships.

topics.name: Developed Informational and Explanatory Writing
topics.description: An explanation introduces a topic, develops related ideas with evidence and helps readers see how the parts connect.
topics.locator: Phase 3 teaching sequence > Writing; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: developed informational and explanatory writing.
evidence: Plans and develops a logical explanation with relevant supporting detail.
misconceptions: A strong explanation is just a collection of interesting unrelated facts.
topics.question: In an explanation of a local waterway, what could follow an opening paragraph about the catchment?
topics.answer: A paragraph explaining how rainwater travels through the catchment, supported by relevant observations or sources.
topics.explanation: The next paragraph develops the topic in a logical direction rather than changing subject.
hints: What process does the introduction raise?
What details could explain how it works?
topics.activity: Plan an explanation with an opening, two logically ordered sections and source notes, then draft one section.

topics.name: Narrative Perspective and Unreliable Narrators
topics.description: A narrator's perspective shapes what readers learn; their account can be limited or unreliable without making every detail false.
topics.locator: Phase 4 teaching sequence > Text Studies; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: narrative perspective and unreliable narrators.
evidence: Uses textual evidence to discuss limits of a narrator's account.
misconceptions: An unreliable narrator necessarily lies about everything.
topics.question: A narrator says, “I never make mistakes,” immediately after misreading a map. What should a reader consider?
topics.answer: The narrator's confident claim conflicts with the event, so their self-assessment may be unreliable.
topics.explanation: The contrast between claim and action is evidence for questioning the narrator's perspective.
hints: What does the narrator claim?
Does the action support that claim?
topics.activity: Write two accounts of a small event from different viewpoints and identify what each narrator can and cannot know.

topics.name: Tracing Theme Across a Text
topics.description: A theme is a developed idea that can emerge through recurring choices, images or events across a text.
topics.locator: Phase 4 teaching sequence > Text Studies; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: tracing theme across a text.
evidence: Supports a thematic interpretation with evidence from more than one part of a text.
misconceptions: A theme is a single topic word with no supported interpretation.
topics.question: A story repeatedly shows characters sharing resources during hardship. What possible theme could a reader test?
topics.answer: A possible theme is that cooperation helps a community through difficulty; the reader should support it with multiple details.
topics.explanation: A theme is an interpretation supported by patterns across the text.
hints: What idea connects the repeated actions?
What evidence from more than one moment would support it?
topics.activity: Track a repeated image or action through a short story and explain how it contributes to a possible theme.

topics.name: Evaluating Arguments in Non-Fiction
topics.description: Evaluating an argument involves identifying its claim, checking the relevance and reliability of evidence and considering alternative explanations.
topics.locator: Phase 4 teaching sequence > Text Studies; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: evaluating arguments in non-fiction.
evidence: Identifies a claim and explains a limitation in its supporting evidence.
misconceptions: A confident claim becomes reliable when it includes any number.
topics.question: An article says a new sign reduced litter because one bin was empty on one day. What is a limitation?
topics.answer: One observation from one bin is not enough to establish a general reduction or the effect of the sign.
topics.explanation: A stronger claim would require a suitable comparison and more representative evidence.
hints: How much was observed?
What else might explain an empty bin?
topics.activity: Compare two short claims, label each claim and its evidence, and propose one way to improve the evidence.

topics.name: Purpose, audience, and context
topics.description: A text's purpose, audience and context can influence its form and language, and readers can use textual evidence to explain those choices.
topics.locator: Phase 4 teaching sequence > Text Studies; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: purpose, audience, and context.
evidence: Explains a relationship between a text feature, audience and purpose.
misconceptions: The same text feature has exactly the same effect in every context.
topics.question: A safety poster uses brief commands and large headings. Why might these choices suit its purpose?
topics.answer: They make important actions quick to find and understand for readers who may have little time.
topics.explanation: The explanation connects features to a plausible audience and purpose.
hints: What action does the poster want readers to take?
How do the headings help someone scanning quickly?
topics.activity: Compare a public notice and a personal message about the same issue and annotate features that suit each audience.

topics.name: Persuasive Writing
topics.description: Persuasive writing makes a reasoned claim, selects evidence, considers counterarguments and adjusts language for its audience.
topics.locator: Phase 4 teaching sequence > Language Studies; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: persuasive writing.
evidence: Supports a claim with reasons and responds to a relevant counterargument.
misconceptions: Ignoring every opposing view automatically makes an argument stronger.
topics.question: A proposal argues for a covered bike rack. What counterargument could it address?
topics.answer: For example, the cost may be a concern; the proposal could compare costs with expected benefits and alternatives.
topics.explanation: Addressing a relevant concern helps readers evaluate the proposal more fully.
hints: What might someone who disagrees worry about?
How could the writer respond with evidence?
topics.activity: Draft a short proposal with a claim, two reasons, a credible supporting source and one fair response to an alternative view.

topics.name: Writing Techniques for Effect
topics.description: Writers deliberately select language and structure to shape meaning, then revise according to the intended effect.
topics.locator: Phase 4 teaching sequence > Language Studies; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: writing techniques for effect.
evidence: Explains how a deliberate language choice contributes to an intended effect.
misconceptions: More elaborate language always improves clarity.
topics.question: Compare “The room was noisy” with “Voices bounced off the walls.” What effect does the second create?
topics.answer: It creates a more vivid sense of surrounding sound through imagery.
topics.explanation: The second sentence invites the reader to imagine the sound rather than simply naming it.
hints: Which words describe how the sound seems to move?
What picture or feeling might that create?
topics.activity: Revise two plain sentences for a chosen audience; explain why each change helps the intended effect.

topics.name: Multimedia Presentations
topics.description: A presentation can combine spoken or signed language, visuals and other modes, with each element selected for its communicative purpose.
topics.locator: Phase 4 teaching sequence > Language Studies; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: multimedia presentations.
evidence: Uses more than one mode purposefully and explains how they work together.
misconceptions: Adding more images or effects always makes a presentation clearer.
topics.question: A graph and a spoken explanation present the same data. What can the speaker add?
topics.answer: The speaker can explain the pattern, units and limitations rather than reading every value aloud.
topics.explanation: Different modes can complement each other when each contributes useful information.
hints: What can the audience see in the graph?
What explanation would help them interpret it?
topics.activity: Create a short presentation with one labelled visual and a spoken, signed or written explanation that adds context and cites the source.

topics.name: Planning, Revising and Editing Writing
topics.description: A writer can plan around a purpose, revise ideas and organisation, and edit language conventions before sharing a text.
topics.locator: Phase 4 teaching sequence > Language Studies; suggested phase-level alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: planning, revising and editing writing.
evidence: Revises organisation and checks conventions for an intended audience.
misconceptions: Correct spelling alone ensures an argument is well organised.
topics.question: A draft argues for more shade but its evidence comes after an unrelated paragraph. What revision would help?
topics.answer: Move the relevant evidence beside the claim, remove or connect the unrelated paragraph, and check the resulting flow.
topics.explanation: Reorganisation strengthens the connection between a claim and its support.
hints: Where is the claim?
Which paragraph contains the supporting evidence?
topics.activity: Exchange a short draft, check claim–evidence order, revise for clarity and then edit sentence-level errors.

topics.name: Explaining a reason with because
topics.description: The word because can connect an event or choice to a reason. A complete explanation tells the listener what happened and why.
topics.locator: Phase 1 (Years 0–3) teaching sequence > Oral Language > Communicating and Presenting > Verbal reasoning; first year at school; phase-wide school-year search band because the official sequence is organised by time at school
objectives: Use speech, sign, drawing or an accessible communication tool to give a reason for a fictional child taking an umbrella.
evidence: Connects a plausible reason to the stated action.
misconceptions: Because tells the listener only what happened, with no reason.
topics.question: Finish the idea: “The ground is wet because …” with a possible reason.
topics.answer: For example: “The ground is wet because it rained.”
topics.explanation: The word because can connect an event or choice to a reason. A complete explanation tells the listener what happened and why.
hints: What happened to the ground?
What event could have made it wet?
topics.activity: Use speech, sign, drawing or an accessible communication tool to give a reason for a fictional child taking an umbrella.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Predicting with if and then
topics.description: An if–then statement connects a possible condition to an outcome. It expresses what may happen when that condition holds.
topics.locator: Phase 1 (Years 0–3) teaching sequence > Oral Language > Communicating and Presenting > Verbal reasoning; first year at school; phase-wide school-year search band because the official sequence is organised by time at school
objectives: Make an if–then prediction about a fictional paper boat in water and share it with a partner.
evidence: States a condition and a possible outcome.

misconceptions: A navigation menu is only a decorative image.
topics.question: What does a navigation menu help a reader do?
topics.answer: Find and move to different sections of a site or digital text.
topics.explanation: Menus and hyperlinks shape how a reader moves through a digital text and finds information.
hints: Does it describe a story character?
How could it help you reach another section?
topics.activity: Sketch a fictional information page with three labelled navigation links and describe where one would lead.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Combining modes to shape a message
topics.description: A digital text can combine writing, visuals and sound. Analysing how they work together helps explain the message and its effect.

objectives: Plan a fictional conservation message using a caption and one visual; explain how they work together.
evidence: Explains a relationship between two modes and an intended effect.
misconceptions: A digital message can communicate only through written words.
topics.question: How might a quiet audio track change the mood of a calm landscape image?
topics.answer: It can reinforce a calm mood, depending on how the sound and image are used.
topics.explanation: A digital text can combine writing, visuals and sound. Analysing how they work together helps explain the message and its effect.
hints: What does the image show?
What feeling might the audio reinforce?
topics.activity: Plan a fictional conservation message using a caption and one visual; explain how they work together.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Whose perspective is missing?
topics.description: A text may include some perspectives and leave others out. Identifying an omission helps readers consider how the account might change.
topics.locator: Phase 3 (Years 7–8) teaching sequence > Reading > Critical Analysis > Interpretations and connections > Year 8
objectives: Annotate a fictional article summary to list included and potentially missing perspectives.
evidence: Identifies a relevant missing perspective and explains why it matters.
misconceptions: A text’s quoted voices always represent everyone affected.
topics.question: An article about a new playground quotes adults but no children. Whose perspective is missing?
topics.answer: Children who may use the playground.
topics.explanation: A text may include some perspectives and leave others out. Identifying an omission helps readers consider how the account might change.
hints: Who is quoted?
Who else is affected by the decision?
topics.activity: Annotate a fictional article summary to list included and potentially missing perspectives.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Adding a relative clause
topics.description: A relative clause adds information about a noun and may begin with who, which or that.
topics.locator: Phase 3 (Years 7–8) teaching sequence > Writing > Composition > Sentence structures, grammar, and punctuation > Year 7
objectives: Add a relative clause to a sentence about a fictional object.
evidence: Identifies the relative clause and the noun it describes.
misconceptions: A relative clause always describes a verb.
topics.question: In “The book that I borrowed is on the desk”, which words add information about book?
topics.answer: “that I borrowed”.
topics.explanation: A relative clause adds information about a noun and may begin with who, which or that.

Which group tells you which book?
topics.activity: Add a relative clause to a sentence about a fictional object.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Compound-complex sentences
topics.description: A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.
topics.locator: Phase 3 (Years 7–8) teaching sequence > Writing > Composition > Sentence structures, grammar, and punctuation > Year 8
objectives: Label the dependent and independent clauses in the supplied sentence, then write a new example.
evidence: Identifies two independent clauses and a dependent clause.
misconceptions: A compound-complex sentence contains only one clause.
topics.question: What are the independent clauses in “Although it rained, we played, and the crowd cheered”?
topics.answer: “we played” and “the crowd cheered”.
topics.explanation: A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.
hints: Which parts could stand as complete sentences?
Which clause begins with Although and depends on another clause?
topics.activity: Label the dependent and independent clauses in the supplied sentence, then write a new example.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Using a semicolon between related clauses
topics.description: A semicolon can link two closely related independent clauses when each could stand as a sentence.
topics.locator: Phase 3 (Years 7–8) teaching sequence > Writing > Composition > Sentence structures, grammar, and punctuation > Years 7–8
objectives: Join two fictional complete ideas with a semicolon and check that both sides can stand alone.
evidence: Uses a semicolon between two related independent clauses.
misconceptions: A semicolon can join any two incomplete fragments.
topics.question: Which punctuation could link these complete, related ideas: “The bell rang” and “the class left”?
topics.answer: A semicolon: “The bell rang; the class left.”
topics.explanation: A semicolon can link two closely related independent clauses when each could stand as a sentence.
hints: Can each side stand alone?
Which punctuation links closely related independent clauses?
topics.activity: Join two fictional complete ideas with a semicolon and check that both sides can stand alone.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: A gerund as a noun
topics.description: A gerund is an –ing form used as a noun. Its role in the sentence determines how it functions.
topics.locator: Phase 3 (Years 7–8) teaching sequence > Writing > Composition > Sentence structures, grammar, and punctuation > Year 8
objectives: Write a sentence in which reading or drawing is the subject and identify the gerund.
evidence: Identifies an –ing form functioning as the sentence subject.
misconceptions: Every word ending in –ing is always the main verb.
topics.question: In “Swimming is enjoyable”, what is the subject of the sentence?
topics.answer: Swimming.
topics.explanation: A gerund is an –ing form used as a noun. Its role in the sentence determines how it functions.
hints: Which word names the activity?
What is enjoyable?
topics.activity: Write a sentence in which reading or drawing is the subject and identify the gerund.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Choosing active or passive voice
topics.description: Active voice places the doer as the grammatical subject; passive voice foregrounds the receiver or action, and may omit the doer.
topics.locator: Phase 3 (Years 7–8) teaching sequence > Writing > Composition > Sentence structures, grammar, and punctuation > Years 7–8
objectives: Rewrite a fictional active sentence in passive voice and explain the change in focus.
evidence: Identifies the receiver of the action and rewrites the sentence accurately.
misconceptions: Passive voice always means the sentence has no verb.
topics.question: In “The cake was decorated by Ana”, which part receives the action?
topics.answer: The cake receives the action; the sentence is passive.
topics.explanation: Active voice places the doer as the grammatical subject; passive voice foregrounds the receiver or action, and may omit the doer.
hints: What was decorated?
Who did the decorating?
topics.activity: Rewrite a fictional active sentence in passive voice and explain the change in focus.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Selecting a synonym for tone
topics.description: Synonyms can overlap in meaning while differing in intensity or tone. A writer chooses the word that fits the intended effect.
topics.locator: Phase 3 (Years 7–8) teaching sequence > Writing > Composition > Audience, purpose, and language choice > Year 8
objectives: Compare three teacher-provided synonyms for a fictional character’s feeling and justify one choice.
evidence: Explains how the selected synonym fits the intended intensity.
misconceptions: Synonyms are interchangeable in every situation.
topics.question: Which sounds stronger: “annoyed” or “furious”?
topics.answer: Furious generally suggests stronger anger.
topics.explanation: Synonyms can overlap in meaning while differing in intensity or tone. A writer chooses the word that fits the intended effect.
hints: Do both words relate to anger?
Which conveys greater intensity?
topics.activity: Compare three teacher-provided synonyms for a fictional character’s feeling and justify one choice.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Dramatic irony in drama
topics.description: Dramatic irony occurs when an audience knows something a character does not, which can create tension or change how a scene is understood.
topics.locator: Phase 4 (Years 9–10) teaching sequence > Text Studies > Textual and Critical Analysis > Features of text > Years 9–10
objectives: Write two lines describing what an audience and a fictional character each know in a scene.
evidence: Explains the difference in knowledge between audience and character.
misconceptions: Dramatic irony simply means any character says something funny.
topics.question: The audience knows a letter is lost, but the character expects it to arrive. What creates dramatic irony?
topics.answer: The audience knows the letter is lost while the character does not.
topics.explanation: Dramatic irony occurs when an audience knows something a character does not, which can create tension or change how a scene is understood.
hints: What does the audience know?
Does the character know the same thing?
topics.activity: Write two lines describing what an audience and a fictional character each know in a scene.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Line breaks and meaning in poetry
topics.description: Lineation is the arrangement of a poem into lines. A line break can control pace, emphasis or the way a reader anticipates the next idea.
topics.locator: Phase 4 (Years 9–10) teaching sequence > Text Studies > Textual and Critical Analysis > Features of text > Years 9–10
objectives: Write a two-line original poem and move the line break; discuss one change in effect.
evidence: Explains how a changed line break affects emphasis or pace.
misconceptions: Poetic line breaks can never influence meaning.
topics.question: Why might a poet place a surprising word at the start of a new line?
topics.answer: The break can give the word emphasis or alter the reader’s pace and expectation.
topics.explanation: Lineation is the arrangement of a poem into lines. A line break can control pace, emphasis or the way a reader anticipates the next idea.
hints: Where does the pause occur?
What happens when the next word appears after the break?
topics.activity: Write a two-line original poem and move the line break; discuss one change in effect.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Film lighting and audience response
topics.description: A filmmaker can use lighting with framing and sound to shape mood and guide an audience’s attention.
topics.locator: Phase 4 (Years 9–10) teaching sequence > Text Studies > Textual and Critical Analysis > Features of text > Years 9–10
objectives: Sketch two fictional versions of the same scene with bright and dim lighting; compare their likely effects.
evidence: Connects a lighting choice to a plausible audience effect.
misconceptions: Lighting only determines whether the camera can record an image.
topics.question: How might dim lighting contribute to a suspenseful scene?
topics.answer: It can limit what the audience sees and support an uncertain or tense mood.
topics.explanation: A filmmaker can use lighting with framing and sound to shape mood and guide an audience’s attention.
hints: How much of the scene is visible?
How could limited visibility affect the viewer?
topics.activity: Sketch two fictional versions of the same scene with bright and dim lighting; compare their likely effects.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Framing in media texts
topics.description: A media text frames an issue by selecting details, images and wording. Readers can compare what different framings emphasise or omit.
topics.locator: Phase 4 (Years 9–10) teaching sequence > Text Studies > Textual and Critical Analysis > Features of text > Years 9–10
objectives: Compare two teacher-created descriptions of a fictional event and identify one difference in emphasis.
evidence: Identifies a difference in selection and explains a possible effect.
misconceptions: Two reports on the same event must frame it identically.
topics.question: Two reports use the same event but choose different photographs. What should a reader compare?
topics.answer: What each photo emphasises or leaves out and how that could influence the audience.
topics.explanation: A media text frames an issue by selecting details, images and wording. Readers can compare what different framings emphasise or omit.
hints: What is visible in each image?
What information or perspective might be outside the frame?
topics.activity: Compare two teacher-created descriptions of a fictional event and identify one difference in emphasis.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Checking misleading information and context
topics.description: False information may be shared by mistake or deliberately; a reader should check the source, evidence and context before deciding what a claim means.

objectives: Investigate a teacher-created fictional post with a supplied date and source card; identify the mismatch.
evidence: Uses the source and date to explain why the claim is misleading.
misconceptions: A false claim alone proves the sharer intended to deceive.
topics.question: A dramatic post shows an old photo as if it were from today. What should you verify?
topics.answer: The photo’s origin and date, the claim, and reliable reporting about the current event.
topics.explanation: False information may be shared by mistake or deliberately; a reader should check the source, evidence and context before deciding what a claim means.
hints: When was the image actually taken?
Does it match the event described in the post?
topics.activity: Investigate a teacher-created fictional post with a supplied date and source card; identify the mismatch.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Connecting literary traditions
topics.description: Authors may draw on more than one literary tradition. Comparison should use evidence from each text and respect the context in which cultural material is shared.

objectives: Compare two teacher-provided, appropriately shared text summaries and document a specific similarity and difference.
evidence: Supports a comparison with details from both texts.
misconceptions: A shared storytelling pattern means two cultures or texts are identical.
topics.question: What evidence would support a claim that two texts use a similar storytelling pattern?
topics.answer: Specific features or passages from both texts showing the similarity.
topics.explanation: Authors may draw on more than one literary tradition. Comparison should use evidence from each text and respect the context in which cultural material is shared.
hints: Which feature appears in the first text?
Where can you find a comparable feature in the second?
topics.activity: Compare two teacher-provided, appropriately shared text summaries and document a specific similarity and difference.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Reconsidering an interpretation
topics.description: A reader can revise an interpretation after rereading or hearing another evidence-based perspective.

objectives: Discuss an original short scene with a partner, then add one note about whether their evidence changed your view.
evidence: Refers to a new detail and explains its effect on an interpretation.
misconceptions: A first interpretation can never be revised.
topics.question: What might a reader do after a classmate points out a detail they missed?
topics.answer: Reconsider their interpretation and explain whether the detail changes it.
topics.explanation: A reader can revise an interpretation after rereading or hearing another evidence-based perspective.

Does it support, complicate or challenge the first interpretation?
topics.activity: Discuss an original short scene with a partner, then add one note about whether their evidence changed your view.

objectives: Write a one-sentence thesis about a teacher-provided fictional scene and list one possible piece of evidence.
evidence: States an arguable interpretation and identifies relevant evidence.
misconceptions: A thesis is only a list of everything that happens in a story.

topics.answer: The second: it makes an arguable interpretation about the character’s choices.

Could examples from the story support that claim?

topics.name: Explaining evidence in a literary essay
topics.description: A quotation or example is useful when the writer explains how it supports the paragraph’s claim and the larger thesis.
topics.locator: Phase 4 (Years 9–10) teaching sequence > Language Studies > Crafting Texts > Literary essays > Year 9
objectives: Use one short quotation from a teacher-provided original scene and write a sentence explaining its relevance to a claim.
evidence: Connects the selected evidence to a specific interpretive claim.
misconceptions: A quotation alone automatically proves any claim.
topics.question: Why add analysis after a quotation in a literary essay?
topics.answer: To explain how the selected evidence supports the writer’s interpretation.
topics.explanation: A quotation or example is useful when the writer explains how it supports the paragraph’s claim and the larger thesis.

What connection should the writer make for the reader?
topics.activity: Use one short quotation from a teacher-provided original scene and write a sentence explaining its relevance to a claim.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Connecting perspectives in discursive writing

topics.explanation: A discursive text explores an issue from multiple angles. Connecting perspectives can show how they agree, differ or qualify one another.

How do the two ideas differ or connect?
topics.activity: Plan a fictional question about school gardens and write one sentence representing each of two views.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Responding to a counterargument

topics.explanation: A counterargument presents a relevant opposing view. A response addresses it with reasoning or evidence rather than ignoring it.
hints: What concern does the opposing view raise?
What evidence could answer that specific concern?
topics.activity: Write one counterargument to a fictional proposal and a respectful evidence-based response.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Evidence and emotional appeals

topics.question: Which is an appeal to evidence: a cited survey result or an unsupported warning that “everyone will panic”?
topics.answer: A relevant, accurately cited survey result can provide evidence.
topics.explanation: Persuasive texts may use reasoning, credible evidence and emotional appeal. These techniques can be examined separately and together.

materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.name: Ethical use of digital material

topics.explanation: Responsible digital creation involves checking claims, crediting sources, respecting permission and considering how people are represented.

topics.explanation: A visual text combines design choices such as framing, contrast and captions to guide attention and communicate with an audience.

How does the caption explain the image?
topics.activity: Sketch a fictional public-information poster and annotate how its caption and image work together.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.explanation: Words with related dictionary meanings can carry different associations. A writer chooses connotations that suit the intended audience and tone.

What different impressions can the words create?
topics.activity: Compare two neutral fictional descriptions and explain the tone of each word choice.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

topics.explanation: A presentation’s form, organisation and delivery should fit its audience and purpose. Speakers can also use signed or supported communication.

What information would make the message clearer?
topics.activity: Plan a brief fictional presentation for a younger audience and define one unfamiliar term.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible communication tool

Does the ending indicate one or more than one here?
topics.activity: Match cat and cats to cards showing one and several cats; explain the ending.

topics.name: Building comfortable writing stamina
